paragraphs.heading: Breaking a fraction apart
paragraphs.text: Partial fraction decomposition takes a rational fraction, a fraction whose top and bottom are both polynomials, and rewrites it as a sum. The sum has a polynomial part, which may be zero, plus one or more fractions whose denominators are simpler. Johann Bernoulli and Gottfried Leibniz each found the idea on their own in 1702.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is useful
paragraphs.text: Splitting a fraction this way gives step-by-step methods for many calculations with rational functions. Among them are working out antiderivatives, expanding into Taylor series, and taking inverse Laplace transforms and inverse Z-transforms. For antiderivatives, the job comes down to integrating a final sum called the logarithmic part, whose antiderivative is a linear combination of logarithms.

paragraphs.heading: First, divide if needed
paragraphs.text: Say the fraction is P(x)/Q(x). If the degree of P is at least the degree of Q, start with polynomial long division, which gives P(x) = E(x) Q(x) + R(x), where the remainder R has lower degree than Q. Dividing through by Q(x) leaves E(x) plus the fraction R(x)/Q(x). The polynomial E(x) is done, and only the leftover fraction R(x)/Q(x) still needs splitting.

paragraphs.heading: What the pieces look like
paragraphs.text: In the finished result, each denominator is a power of an irreducible polynomial, one that cannot be factored into polynomials of positive degree. Each numerator has lower degree than that irreducible polynomial. Over the complex numbers, the fundamental theorem of algebra makes every such polynomial degree one, so every numerator is a constant. Over the real numbers some may be quadratic, so pieces with a linear top over a power of a quadratic can also appear.

paragraphs.heading: Hermite's method
paragraphs.text: One simple way to compute the pieces is Hermite's method. First, find the polynomial part by Euclidean division, which leaves a fraction whose top has lower degree than its bottom. Since the degree of each unknown numerator is known, write each one as a polynomial with unknown coefficients. Then bring all the pieces to a common denominator and match the coefficient of each power of x on the two sides, which gives a system of linear equations whose solution is the unique answer.

paragraphs.heading: A coarser, easier version
paragraphs.text: When the work is done explicitly, a coarser version is often preferred, using square-free polynomials in place of irreducible ones. This swaps full factorization for the much easier square-free factorization. It is enough for most applications, and when the input coefficients are integers or rational numbers it avoids bringing in irrational ones.

paragraphs.heading: Why the answer is unique
paragraphs.text: The decomposition always exists, which can be shown by applying a few reduction steps over and over, built on Euclidean division and Bézout's identity. It is also unique. The shape of the decomposition defines a linear map, and the existence proof shows this map is surjective; since the two vector spaces involved have the same dimension, it is injective too. That argument doubles as an algorithm that finds the decomposition with linear algebra.
